newsitem.title: USA: Conrail merger talks progress, deal seen soon.
newsitem.headline: Conrail merger talks progress, deal seen soon.

text.p: A four-month-old battle for control of Conrail Inc may be resolved soon with an agreement that calls for the railroad's assets to be split between rival bidders CSX Corp and Norfolk Southern Corp, according to sources familiar with the situation.

The sources, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said negotiations to end the takeover fight have gained momentum and it increasingly appears a negotiated deal will be struck between the three parties.
"I do believe it is going to happen quite soon," said one source who is close to the negotiations.

Conrail and CSX orginally agreed to merge in October, but the $9.4 billion cash and stock pact has been stymied since January when Conrail shareholders rejected a critical measure that would have permitted the transaction to move forward. Many of the shareholders favor Norfolk Southern's $10.5 billion cash offer for Conrail.

Top executives of the three railraods met on January 31 to discuss the stalemate, but declined to comment on the nature of the talks or on future meetings. Since then, the three companies have refused to comment on the situation and it was not immediately clear if executives of all three companies have participated in subsequent discussions.
Under the merger pact now in place between Conrail and CSX, neither party can discuss another transaction with a third company until 1999 without mutual approval.
The sources said several proposals may be considered, including a potential joint bid for Conrail.

Although the talks remain extremely delicate, the sources said that both CSX and Norfolk Southern acknowledge that neither will succeed in winning Conrail alone. Furthermore, the sources said that Conrail, which previously had opposed a division of its assets, now believes that will be the most likely outcome.

"There has been the growing recognition that a stalemate is the worst alternative for everybody. The parties realize that the only way to solve it is to do something that will involve all three parties," said another source who also is close to the companies.
Norfolk Southern and Conrail declined to comment on the situation. CSX could not immediately be reached for comment.

Meanwhile, both rival bidders have been pursuing their separate transactions even as negotiations are occurring privately. Norfolk Southern recently bought 9.9 percent of Conrail and both companies soon expect to file their offers with the Surface Transportation Board, the federal agency that oversees railroads.
